propositions.text: This appeal concerns interpretation and application of the Patented Medicines Regulations linking patent rights to market access for subsequent entry drugs.
propositions.quote: This appeal concerns the interpretation and application of the Patented Medicines (Notice of Compliance) Regulations, S.O.R./93-133 (the Regulations), which link patent rights in medicines to market access for subsequent entry (generic or biosimilar) versions of those medicines.

propositions.text: Specifically, the appeal concerns timing of adding patents to the Patent Register that second persons must address for market access.
propositions.quote: Specifically, this appeal concerns the timing of the addition of patents to the register defined in the Regulations (the Patent Register) that a second person must address when seeking market access (a notice of compliance (NOC)) for a subsequent entry drug.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appeal concerns interpretation of the Regulations linking patent rights to market access, specifically timing of patent additions to the Patent Register.

propositions.text: The appellant Bayer submitted a patent list and drug submissions for EYLEA on August 22, 2023.
propositions.quote: The appellant, Bayer Inc. (Bayer, a first person under the Regulations), submitted a patent list in relation to its Canadian Patent No. 2,970,315 (the 315 Patent) and drug submissions for its drug EYLEA (containing the medicinal ingredient aflibercept) on August 22, 2023;

propositions.text: OSIP found the 315 Patent eligible for inclusion on the Patent Register on August 30, 2023.
propositions.quote: The Office of Submissions and Intellectual Property (OSIP) of Health Canada, on behalf of the Minister of Health (the Minister), reviewed Bayer’s submission and found the 315 Patent eligible for inclusion on the Patent Register on August 30, 2023;

propositions.text: The respondent Amgen filed a new drug submission for its subsequent entry version on August 24, 2023.
propositions.quote: In the interim, the respondent Amgen Canada Inc. (Amgen, a second person under the Regulations) filed a new drug submission (NDS) for its subsequent entry version of aflibercept on August 24, 2023;

propositions.text: OSIP decided Amgen’s NDS was administratively complete on August 31, 2023, but treated August 24 as filing date.
propositions.quote: Though the OSIP decided only on August 31, 2023 that Amgen’s NDS was administratively complete, it treated the date of submission thereof (August 24, 2023) as its filing date.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the facts: Bayer submitted patent list August 22, OSIP found patent eligible August 30, Amgen filed NDS August 24, OSIP treated August 24 as filing date.

propositions.text: Because the 315 Patent was not on the Patent Register on August 24, OSIP concluded Amgen need not address it in its NDS.
propositions.quote: Because the 315 Patent had not yet been added to the Patent Register on August 24, 2023, the OSIP concluded that section 5 of the Regulations did not oblige Amgen to address the 315 Patent in its NDS.

propositions.text: OSIP relied on subsection 5(4) which exempts second persons from addressing patents added on or after their NDS filing date.
propositions.quote: The OSIP relied on subsection 5(4) of the Regulations, which provides that a second person need not address a patent that is added to the Patent Register on or after the date of filing of its NDS.

paragraphs.summary: The court states OSIP concluded Amgen need not address the 315 Patent as it was not on the Register on August 24, relying on subsection 5(4).

propositions.text: Bayer sought judicial review of OSIP Decision before Federal Court, which dismissed the application.
propositions.quote: Bayer sought judicial review of this decision by the OSIP (the OSIP Decision) before the Federal Court. However, the application for judicial review was dismissed by Justice James W. O’Reilly (2025 FC 107, the FC Decision).

paragraphs.summary: The court states Bayer sought judicial review of OSIP Decision, which the Federal Court dismissed.

propositions.text: Bayer now appeals the Federal Court Decision to this Court.
propositions.quote: Bayer now appeals the FC Decision to this Court.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Bayer appeals the Federal Court Decision to this Court.

propositions.text: The standard of review is an important hurdle: this Court must determine if Federal Court identified and applied the correct standard to OSIP Decision.
propositions.quote: An important hurdle for Bayer in this appeal concerns the standard of review. Since this is an appeal of a decision of the Federal Court on a judicial review, our task is to determine whether the Federal Court identified the appropriate standard of review to assess the OSIP Decision, and whether the Federal Court applied that standard of review correctly: Agraira v. Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2013 SCC 36, [2013] 2 S.C.R. 559 at para. 45 (Agraira).

propositions.text: This Court must step into the shoes of the Federal Court on standard of review: Agraira at para. 46.
propositions.quote: In other words, we must step into the shoes of the Federal Court: Agraira at para. 46.

propositions.text: Appellant bears strong burden to show Federal Court’s reasoning is flawed if it gave a complete answer to appellant’s arguments: Bank of Montreal v. Canada at para. 4.
propositions.quote: Where the Federal Court appears to have given a complete answer to all the arguments that the appellant advances, the appellant bears a strong tactical burden to show on appeal that the Federal Court’s reasoning is flawed: Bank of Montreal v. Canada (Attorney General), 2021 FCA 189, [2021] D.T.C. 5111 at para. 4.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the standard of review issue and the burden on Bayer to show Federal Court erred in applying it.

propositions.text: Federal Court identified reasonableness as the standard of review and Bayer does not dispute this.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court identified reasonableness as the appropriate standard of review and Bayer does not take issue with that aspect of the FC Decision.

propositions.text: Bayer argues that only one plausible interpretation exists, so correctness and reasonableness standards lead to same result.
propositions.quote: Instead, Bayer argues that the identification of the standard of review is unimportant since there is only one plausible interpretation of the provisions in issue of the Regulations, and so correctness and reasonableness lead to the same result, as discussed in Galderma Canada Inc. v. Canada (Attorney General), 2024 FCA 208, 210 C.P.R. (4th) 181 at para. 17.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Federal Court chose reasonableness standard, which Bayer accepts but argues only one plausible interpretation exists.

propositions.text: This Court must consider whether OSIP Decision met reasonableness as per Vavilov.
propositions.quote: Despite this argument by Bayer, this Court’s task remains to consider whether the OSIP Decision met the requirements of reasonableness as discussed in Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65, [2019] 4 S.C.R. 653 (Vavilov).

propositions.text: The Court concludes OSIP Decision was reasonable and appeal should be dismissed.
propositions.quote: I have concluded that it did, and that this appeal should be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court states it must assess OSIP Decision’s reasonableness and concludes it was reasonable, dismissing the appeal.

propositions.text: Bayer argues OSIP’s interpretation is unreasonable and incorrect regarding dates for NDS filing and patent addition.
propositions.quote: Bayer argues that the OSIP’s interpretation of the Regulations is both unreasonable and incorrect in that the date of filing of Amgen’s NDS was determined to be the date that it was submitted to OSIP (without regard to the date it was later found to be compliant), whereas the date the 315 Patent was determined to be included on the Patent Register was the date it was found to be eligible for inclusion (and not the earlier date when Bayer filed its submission).

propositions.text: Bayer argues Regulations do not contemplate time passage between submission and addition to Patent Register; addition should be on submission day.
propositions.quote: Bayer notes that the Regulations do not contemplate any passage of time between the filing of a submission for an addition to the Patent Register and the actual addition to the Patent Register, and therefore the addition should be considered to have occurred on the day of the submission, regardless of when eligibility was confirmed.

propositions.text: Bayer argues other interpretations disturb balance between innovators and biosimilars the Regulations seek to achieve.
propositions.quote: Bayer argues that any other interpretation disturbs the balance between the interests of innovators and biosimilars that the Regulations strive to achieve.

paragraphs.summary: Bayer argues OSIP’s interpretation is unreasonable, that addition date should be submission date, to preserve balance between innovators and biosimilars.

propositions.text: Bayer argues Amgen would not be prejudiced by applying its interpretation because Amgen could amend its NDS to address patents added after filing.
propositions.quote: Bayer notes that Amgen would not have been prejudiced by its proposed interpretation of the Regulations because it would have been able to amend its NDS to address any patent that was confirmed to have been added to the Patent Register after it filed its NDS.

paragraphs.summary: Bayer argues Amgen would not be prejudiced by its interpretation as Amgen could amend its NDS to address later-added patents.

propositions.text: Bayer uses race metaphor: either submission date or eligibility date should apply equally to both first and second persons.
propositions.quote: Bayer employs the metaphor of a race between the innovator (the first person) to add its patent to the Patent Register and the biosimilar (the second person) to file its NDS before the first person’s patent is listed on the Patent Register.

propositions.text: Bayer argues it won the race and should prevail; it is unreasonable to apply earlier date to Amgen but not Bayer.
propositions.quote: Bayer argues that, either the date of submission should apply to both, or the date of the OSIP’s determination (of eligibility or compliance, as the case may be) should apply to both the first and second persons. In either case, Bayer argues, it won the race and should prevail in this case. It argues that it was unbalanced and unreasonable to apply the earlier date to Amgen’s NDS but not to Bayer’s patent list submission.

paragraphs.summary: Bayer argues the date applied should be the same for both parties, and it won the race, so OSIP’s approach is unbalanced and unreasonable.

propositions.text: Bayer notes second person has access to public info about patent listing, but first person lacks info about second person’s NDS until after filing.
propositions.quote: Bayer also notes that a second person has access to public information about the impending issuance of a patent that might be added to the Patent Register, whereas a first person has no access to information concerning the filing of an NDS by a second person until after the NDS has been filed and found to be administratively complete.

propositions.text: Bayer cites this as another example of imbalance in the Regulations from OSIP’s interpretation.
propositions.quote: Bayer cites this as another example of imbalance in the Regulations resulting from the OSIP’s interpretation.

paragraphs.summary: Bayer argues second persons have public info advantage over first persons, causing imbalance under OSIP’s interpretation.

propositions.text: Bayer challenges OSIP and Federal Court reliance on Eli Lilly case, which confirmed patent added on eligibility date, not submission date.
propositions.quote: Finally, Bayer takes issue with the OSIP’s and the Federal Court’s reliance on Eli Lilly Canada Inc. v. Canada (Attorney General), 2009 FC 474, [2009] F.C.J. No. 587 (Eli Lilly). In Eli Lilly, the Federal Court confirmed the Minister’s conclusion that a patent was added to the Patent Register as of the date it was found to be eligible to be listed, and not the date of the submission of the patent list.

propositions.text: Eli Lilly facts differed: patent initially found ineligible, later reversed after more info; patent listing date not submission date.
propositions.quote: The facts in Eli Lilly differed somewhat from the facts in the present appeal in that the patent in Eli Lilly was initially found to be ineligible for listing. That conclusion by the Minister was later reversed after additional information was provided by Eli Lilly.

propositions.text: Eli Lilly requested patent be considered listed as of submission date; Minister refused; Federal Court upheld distinction between submission and addition.
propositions.quote: Eli Lilly then asked that the patent in issue be considered to have been listed as of the date of the submission of the patent list. The refusal of that request by the Minister was later upheld by the Federal Court on the basis that there is a distinction between submitting a patent to be added to the Patent Register, and the actual addition of the patent to the Patent Register.

propositions.text: Federal Court recognized risk of time difference disadvantaging innovator but said it was a legislative choice inherent in Regulations.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court recognized that its interpretation of the Regulations resulted in a risk of a time difference between the two events that could work to the innovator’s (the first person’s) disadvantage, but that this was a legislative choice that was inherent in the Regulations.

paragraphs.summary: Bayer argues Eli Lilly case is distinguishable and confirms patent added on eligibility date, not submission date, a legislative choice.

propositions.text: Bayer argues Eli Lilly is not binding, distinguishable, and unpersuasive for several reasons.
propositions.quote: Bayer argues that Eli Lilly is not binding on this Court, and that it is distinguishable and unpersuasive.

propositions.text: Bayer notes no intervening NDS was filed during patent listing pendency in Eli Lilly, unlike here.
propositions.quote: Bayer notes that, contrary to the present case, no intervening NDS was filed by a second person during the pendency of the request to add the patent to the Patent Register in Eli Lilly.

propositions.text: Bayer notes Eli Lilly lacks discussion of reliability of patent list certification under paragraph 4(4)(f).
propositions.quote: Bayer also notes that Eli Lilly includes no discussion of the reliability of a patent list submitted by a first person as a result of the requirement of paragraph 4(4)(f) of the Regulations for the first person to certify that the patent list is eligible for listing.

propositions.text: Bayer notes subsection 3(2.3) empowering Minister to review patent listings was not in force at Eli Lilly time.
propositions.quote: Bayer further notes that subsection 3(2.3) of the Regulations, which empowers the Minister to review the listing of any patents in the Patent Register, was not yet in force when Eli Lilly was decided.

propositions.text: Bayer argues Minister now has tool to remove wrongly added patents, unlike at Eli Lilly time.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the Minister now has a tool that was not available when Eli Lilly was decided, which allows the Minister to remove a patent from the Patent Register that should not have been added.

paragraphs.summary: Bayer argues Eli Lilly is not binding and distinguishable because no intervening NDS, no certification discussion, and new Minister powers exist now.

propositions.text: Bayer’s arguments improperly ask Court to interpret Regulations instead of focusing on OSIP’s interpretation, contrary to Vavilov guidance.
propositions.quote: The main problem with most of Bayer’s arguments is that they effectively ask this Court to engage in its own interpretation of the Regulations instead of focusing on the OSIP’s interpretation. This is contrary to the guidance of paragraphs 83 and 84 of Vavilov.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Bayer improperly asks it to interpret Regulations rather than focus on OSIP’s interpretation, contrary to Vavilov.

propositions.text: OSIP Decision is detailed, 27 pages, summarizing facts, framework, and interpretive analysis relevant to appeal.
propositions.quote: I note first that the OSIP Decision comprises some 27 pages of tightly spaced text. It contains a detailed summary of the facts, as well as a description of the framework of the Regulations and an interpretive analysis of the provisions thereof that are relevant to this appeal.

propositions.text: OSIP reached decision after considering parties’ submissions on a preliminary decision, which itself considered parties’ submissions.
propositions.quote: I note also that the OSIP reached its decision after considering submissions from the parties on a preliminary decision, which itself was prepared after considering submissions from the parties.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes OSIP Decision is detailed and based on parties’ submissions on preliminary and final decisions.

propositions.text: Bayer does not assert OSIP failed to consider its submissions but disagrees with OSIP’s conclusions.
propositions.quote: Bayer’s arguments do not assert that the OSIP Decision failed to consider its submissions. Rather, Bayer’s arguments essentially express disagreement with OSIP’s conclusions.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Bayer does not claim OSIP ignored its submissions but disagrees with OSIP’s conclusions.

propositions.text: OSIP Decision’s analysis of sections 3,4,5 concludes patent list is added to Patent Register on eligibility decision date, not submission date, and is reasonable.
propositions.quote: From pages 9 to 16, the OSIP Decision presents a detailed analysis of the text, context and purpose of sections 3, 4 and 5 of the Regulations, and concludes that a patent list, if determined to be eligible, is added to the Patent Register as of the date of the eligibility decision, and not before. Having read this analysis, I find it eminently reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds OSIP’s detailed analysis concluding patent added on eligibility decision date is eminently reasonable.

propositions.text: OSIP described Minister’s duty under subsection 3(2) to ensure only eligible patents are added to Patent Register and detailed eligibility requirements of section 4.
propositions.quote: The OSIP described the duty of the Minister pursuant to subsection 3(2) of the Regulations to ensure that only patents that are eligible for listing pursuant to section 4 are added to the Patent Register. The OSIP also described the detailed eligibility requirements of section 4.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes OSIP described Minister’s duty to add only eligible patents and detailed eligibility requirements.

propositions.text: OSIP concluded Regulations do not require adding patent on submission date or immediate eligibility assessment, nor retroactive effect of eligibility decision.
propositions.quote: The OSIP concluded that the Regulations do not direct it to add a patent to the Patent Register on the date the patent list is submitted to the OSIP, or require it to assess eligibility immediately upon submission. The OSIP also noted that nothing in the Regulations directs retroactive effect of a patent eligibility decision.

propositions.text: This discussion reasonably answers Bayer’s argument that Regulations do not contemplate time passage between submission and addition.
propositions.quote: In my view, this discussion reasonably answered Bayer’s argument that the Regulations do not contemplate any passage of time between filing a patent list and adding a patent to the Patent Register.

propositions.text: Two other patent lists Bayer submitted on August 22, 2023 were found ineligible, emphasizing need for eligibility review before adding patents.
propositions.quote: Moreover, two other patent lists that Bayer submitted to the OSIP on August 22, 2023 in relation to EYLEA were found to be ineligible. This serves to emphasize the need for the OSIP to review eligibility prior to adding a patent to the Patent Register, which review cannot be instantaneous.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds OSIP reasonably concluded Regulations do not require immediate addition or retroactive effect; eligibility review is necessary and not instantaneous.

propositions.text: OSIP’s analysis of subsections 5(1) and 5(2.1) of the Regulations is particularly illuminating
propositions.quote: I find the OSIP’s analysis of the text of subsections 5(1) and 5(2.1) of the Regulations particularly illuminating.

propositions.text: Subsection 5(1) requires a second person filing a notice of compliance submission to include statements or allegations per subsection (2.1) if comparing to another drug with a patent list
propositions.quote: 5 (1) If a second person files a submission for a notice of compliance in respect of a drug and the submission directly or indirectly compares the drug with, or makes reference to, another drug marketed in Canada under a notice of compliance issued to a first person and in respect of which a patent list has been submitted, the second person shall include in the submission the required statements or allegations set out in subsection (2.1).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds OSIP's analysis of subsections 5(1) and 5(2.1) illuminating, quoting subsection 5(1) of the Regulations.

propositions.text: Subsection 5(1) refers to a patent list submitted, but subsection 5(2.1) limits requirements to patents included on the register
propositions.quote: Though subsection 5(1) refers to a patent list that has been submitted, the requirements for the second person filing an NDS are stated to be those set out in subsection 5(2.1), and these are limited to patents that are “included on the register”

propositions.text: Subsection 5(2.1) requires statements or allegations only for each patent included on the register and certificates of supplementary protection included on the register
propositions.quote: 5(2.1) The statements or allegations required for the submission or the supplement, as the case may be, are — with respect to each patent included on the register in respect of the other drug and with respect to each certificate of supplementary protection in which the patent is set out and that is included on the register in respect of the other drug — the following…

paragraphs.summary: The court finds subsection 5(1) refers to a patent list, but subsection 5(2.1) limits requirements to patents included on the register, quoting subsection 5(2.1).

propositions.text: Subsection 5(4) excludes patents added to the Patent Register on or after the date of filing of the second person's NDS, known as the 'frozen register'
propositions.quote: Moreover, subsection 5(4) explicitly excludes from the requirements for the second person any patents that are added to the Patent Register on or after the date of filing of its NDS. This is often referred to as the “frozen register”.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds subsection 5(4) excludes patents added after the second person's NDS filing date, called the 'frozen register'.

propositions.text: OSIP’s interpretation disadvantages Bayer because Amgen filed its NDS while Bayer’s patent list was under consideration
propositions.quote: Though the OSIP’s interpretation of the Regulations clearly disadvantages Bayer in this case because Amgen filed its NDS in the period during which Bayer’s patent list was being considered, and hence Amgen was not required to address the 315 Patent

propositions.text: OSIP was aware of this issue and considered it in its analysis
propositions.quote: the OSIP was well aware of this issue and considered it as part of its analysis.

propositions.text: Bayer argues the only plausible interpretation is that a patent is added to the Patent Register on the date of submission of the patent list
propositions.quote: I am not convinced by Bayer’s argument that the only plausible interpretation of the provisions in issue of the Regulations is that a patent is added to the Patent Register on the date of submission of the patent list.

propositions.text: The court rejects Bayer’s metaphor of a race between the first and second person as inapt
propositions.quote: I do not accept that Bayer’s metaphor of a race between the first person and the second person is apt.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds OSIP’s interpretation disadvantages Bayer but is sound; rejects Bayer’s argument and metaphor about patent addition timing.

propositions.text: OSIP cited the Regulatory Impact Analysis Statement and Health Canada’s Guidance Document supporting that a patent is added to the Patent Register only after eligibility confirmation
propositions.quote: the OSIP Decision cited the Regulatory Impact Analysis Statement (RIAS) that accompanied the 2006 amendments to the Regulations, Regulatory Impact Analysis Statement, Canada Gazette, Part II, Vol. 140, No. 21, S.O.R./2006-242, as well as Health Canada’s Guidance Document for the Regulations.

propositions.text: OSIP concluded a second person’s NDS need not address patents added after the NDS filing date
propositions.quote: The OSIP quoted passages from both of these documents that lead to the conclusion that a patent is considered added to the Patent Register only once its eligibility has been confirmed, and that a second person’s NDS need not address any patents that are added to the Patent Register after the NDS has been filed.

paragraphs.summary: OSIP cited RIAS and Guidance Document concluding patents are added after eligibility confirmation and second person’s NDS need not address later patents.

propositions.text: OSIP stated section 5 would be skewed if a subsequent entry drug manufacturer had to address patents before eligibility determination or retroactively
propositions.quote: …section 5 would not operate as intended and the balance underlying the [Regulations] would be skewed if a subsequent entry drug manufacturer would be required to address a patent on a patent list added to the Patent Register prior to determining patent eligibility or retroactively after determining patent eligibility, and as of the date the patent list is submitted by a first person in respect of a corresponding reference product.

propositions.text: A subsequent entry drug manufacturer only knows a patent is added once it is on the Patent Register, which excludes unassessed patent lists
propositions.quote: A subsequent entry drug manufacturer only knows that a patent on a patent list has been submitted by a first person for inclusion on the Patent Register once that patent is added to the Patent Register. The Patent Register does not include, in accordance with subsection 3(2) of the [Regulations], patent lists submitted by first persons, but not yet assessed for eligibility against the requirements in sections 3 and 4 of the [Regulations].

propositions.text: The Patent Register serves a notice function and the scheme contemplates NDS filing while patent eligibility is under consideration
propositions.quote: The Patent Register serves a notice function for a subsequent entry drug manufacturer at the time of filing of its drug submission and is required for the proper functioning of the scheme. A subsequent entry drug manufacturer cannot predict with certainty what steps the first person and the OSIP will take regarding a patent on a patent list, and therefore, the scheme necessarily contemplates the possibility of a subsequent entry drug submission being filed while the eligibility of a patent on a patent list in respect of the reference product is still under consideration.

propositions.text: The scheme allows patents added later to the register and potentially infringed, but such patents should not preclude NOC issuance to subsequent entry drug manufacturers
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the scheme, specifically the “frozen” Patent Register, contemplates that there may be a patent on a patent list that is later added to the Patent Register and potentially infringed by a subsequent entry drug manufacturer who receives an NOC and markets its version of the reference product. However, the policy choice made by the Governor in Council was that such a patent on a patent list should not preclude the issuance of the NOC to the subsequent entry drug manufacturer for its version of the reference product as there is recourse for the first person under the Patent Act.

paragraphs.summary: OSIP found section 5’s purpose is to avoid requiring subsequent entry drug manufacturers to address patents before eligibility is confirmed, allowing NOC issuance despite later added patents.

propositions.text: The court finds OSIP’s discussion reasonable
propositions.quote: In my view, this discussion is reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds OSIP’s discussion reasonable.

propositions.text: OSIP discussed and adopted Eli Lilly’s analysis of the effective date of addition to the Patent Register
propositions.quote: The OSIP Decision also discussed Eli Lilly, quoting extensively from, and adopting, its analysis of the effective date of an addition to the Patent Register.

propositions.text: OSIP was aware of amendments after Eli Lilly but found its teachings still instructive
propositions.quote: The OSIP was aware of amendments to the Regulations after Eli Lilly but concluded that its teachings remained instructive.

propositions.text: The court sees no error in OSIP’s reasoning on this point
propositions.quote: I see no error in this reasoning.

paragraphs.summary: OSIP adopted Eli Lilly’s analysis on patent register addition date; court sees no error in this reasoning.

propositions.text: Federal Court rejected Bayer’s arguments that OSIP Decision was unreasonable
propositions.quote: On judicial review, the Federal Court rejected Bayer’s arguments that the OSIP Decision was unreasonable.

propositions.text: Federal Court cited OSIP’s discussions of RIAS, Guidance Document and Eli Lilly and found them reasonable
propositions.quote: The Federal Court Decision also cited the OSIP’s discussions of the RIAS accompanying the 2006 amendments to the Regulations, the Guidance Document and Eli Lilly, and found them to be reasonable.

propositions.text: The court finds no error in the Federal Court’s conclusion
propositions.quote: Again, I find no error in this conclusion.

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court found OSIP’s decision reasonable; this court finds no error in that conclusion.

propositions.text: The court dismisses the appeal and awards costs to the respondents of $4,500 each
propositions.quote: For the foregoing reasons, I would dismiss the present appeal. Based on the agreement of the parties, I would award costs to the respondents in the all-inclusive amount of $4,500 each.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal and awards costs to the respondents as agreed.
